title: I just released the demo of my horror card game on itch.io
author: SalivaSpittingWorm
selftext:
Hi, I just put the demo of my game Monstrositas on itch.io. It's a black-and-white horror card game: you died, you're in Hell, and you play cards against demons for a chance at reincarnation. Lose and they eat you.

It's free and runs in the browser. I'd really appreciate it if you tried it and told me what you think, good or bad. The whole game was coded with Claude Code in Godot. Art is from Codex, music is mine from Suno.

[https://cynicz01.itch.io/monstrositas](https://cynicz01.itch.io/monstrositas)

comments.author: Beneficial_Feed_2595
comments.body: Doesn’t work on phone. Cool asthetic.

replies.author: SalivaSpittingWorm
replies.body: Thank you! Yes, it's PC-only for now—it requires a mouse. But given the traffic I'm seeing from mobile devices, I'll start working on a mobile version. Thank you for your interest. :)

replies.author: Beneficial_Feed_2595
replies.body:
It crashes on me halfway through then when I reloaded wouldn’t let me press tutorial button.

Love the writing!!! This has such a vibe! That said the staticy background was too busy, I’d dial back the contrast by like 50% so it’s not so overwhelming. Id love some color even if only an accent here or there. The black and white plus high contrast is an immaculate vibe but visually too stimulating not sure if I could spend hours in that world.

replies.author: SalivaSpittingWorm
replies.body: I'll look into why this happened. It's probably a memory leak. I'll start working on it. I'm not very experienced, so it's a process of trial and error. I'll let you know once I fix it. Hopefully, it'll be okay then. As for the drawing style, I don't know if I'll redo it. It would be a lot of work—it's not like coding. But I'll see if there's anything I can do about it, maybe through the game settings.

replies.author: SalivaSpittingWorm
replies.body: The crash on mobile was a memory leak: the game kept loading images and never let go of them. That should be fixed now, so I hope it won't crash on you again. I also turned down the contrast of the background a bit, and there's now a Background contrast option in the settings, so you can set it however you like.

replies.author: SalivaSpittingWorm
replies.body: If you still want to try the game, you can now play it on your phone. :)

comments.author: challah
comments.body:
I beat it. Some thoughts:

- great art style, on both the game and the cards
- the cards that feature people have an AI look to them (eg Bricks under the bed). I would edit these
- the Play and Back buttons were not clear the first time. Make the cards draggable
- I think the card design/balance needs a lot of work. The main feature is the type triangle. This makes the game all about tempo – whoever goes first has a huge advantage because they can attack with the best counter. This is made worse by only being able to play one creature per turn. The comeback mechanics are Swift and the spells. Drawing them is rng dependent. 
- the lack of resources (eg mana, energy) means that all cards effectively have the same cost. Some cards are objectively stronger than others without any drawbacks.

replies.author: SalivaSpittingWorm
replies.body: Thank you so much for the feedback. I’ll definitely take a look at it. I’ll try to balance the game better. And I’ll check out those cards you mentioned, too. I tried to maintain a consistent style, but it’s possible that something slipped past me. When you’re staring at it for several hours a day, you stop noticing certain things. :)

replies.author: SalivaSpittingWorm
replies.body: Cards in your hand are now draggable, so you can drag them straight onto the table instead of using Play and Back. Stronger monsters now cost more: monsters with 4–6 Power need one sacrifice and monsters with 7+ need two. Weaker cards stay free, so big cards aren't just strictly better anymore. To soften the first-player advantage, the first monster played by whoever starts is still waking up and can't attack on the next turn. I'll take a look at the card designs later :)

replies.author: challah
replies.body: what is the sacrifice mechanic? I don't see it as a cost on a card. I also don't see how many sacrifices I have

replies.author: SalivaSpittingWorm
replies.body: I swear, whenever you fix one thing, something else breaks. This was supposed to be in the tutorial. I’ll fix it when I get home from work. For now, here’s how it works: Monsters with a power of 1–3 are free. A monster with a power of 4–6 costs one of your monsters on the table as a sacrifice, and a monster with a power of 7 or higher costs two.

comments.author: glimsky
comments.body: Loved the art. What was the process for generating it?

replies.author: SalivaSpittingWorm
replies.body:
Thank you! The art was made with Codex (using ImageGen), with me directing it step by step. The process for the characters went roughly like this:

First a full drawing of the seated character. The hatching style came from the game's background: short, irregular white strokes and deep black areas. The drawing was split into separate pieces (body, head, beard, gills...) that fit back together pixel-perfect. Each piece got several hatching frames. Strokes were swapped one by one for similar-sized ones, so the shading stays the same but the lines move. The expressions (talking, grinning, blinking) were edited directly in the original strokes, so the head doesn't jump when the character speaks. In the game, body and head switch frames together every 220 ms, which makes the drawing look alive, like chalk. The appearing animation is 10 frames where white strokes from the background gather into the character's shape.

It took a lot of back and forth, but I was very satisfied with the result. :)

replies.author: SalivaSpittingWorm
replies.body: It's basically the old "line boil" technique from hand-drawn animation, combined with cut-out animation, just done with AI tools.
